practical_skills: Adjusting withholding after a refund or bill

sections.skill: Compare tax liability with withholding to find a refund or balance due, and interpret refunds correctly

questions.prompt: Omar's total tax for the year is $4,560. His employer withheld $5,200. What happens when he files?
questions.intro: Your tax liability is the total tax you owe for the year. Withholding and estimated payments are prepayments. If prepayments are more than the liability, you get a refund; if less, you owe the difference (a balance due).
sources: IRS: Individual returns are generally due April 15 (next business day if on a weekend or holiday); an extension extends the time to file, not to pay; IRS Free File and VITA offer free filing help to eligible taxpayers. (https://www.irs.gov/filing)

questions.prompt: Kim says, "I got a $1,200 refund — free money from the government!" Which statement is accurate?

choices.text: The refund is her own overpaid tax being returned
The refund is a bonus on top of her pay
A big refund means she paid less tax
Refunds are loans from the IRS that must be repaid later

questions.correct_answer: The refund is her own overpaid tax being returned
questions.intro: A refund means too much was withheld during the year. The size of the refund is not the same as how much tax you paid; your actual tax is your liability.
questions.feedback: A refund returns money she already paid through withholding.

misconceptions.B: Assumes a tax refund represents free additional income

sources: IRS: Individual returns are generally due April 15 (next business day if on a weekend or holiday); an extension extends the time to file, not to pay; IRS Free File and VITA offer free filing help to eligible taxpayers. (https://www.irs.gov/filing)

questions.prompt: Kim's $1,200 refund means about $100 a month was over-withheld. If she had kept that $100 a month in a savings account at 4%, roughly how much interest might she have earned over the year (about half a year on average)?
questions.intro: Over-withholding is like an interest-free loan to the government. Adjusting your W-4 can put that money in each paycheck instead.
questions.feedback: About $1,200 × 0.04 × 0.5 ≈ $24, a small but real opportunity cost.

misconceptions.C: Uses the full year on all $1,200

questions.prompt: Leo owed $560 at filing. To avoid that next year with 26 paychecks, about how much extra should he have withheld per paycheck (nearest dollar)?
questions.intro: If you owed at filing, you can add extra withholding on Form W-4 (Step 4(c)) to spread the amount across paychecks.
questions.feedback: $560 ÷ 26 ≈ $21.54, about $22 per paycheck.

misconceptions.D: Puts it all in one check

questions.prompt: Kim got a $1,200 refund and would rather have money in each paycheck. What should she do?

choices.text: Ask the IRS to send her a smaller refund
Update her W-4 so less is withheld

questions.correct_answer: Update her W-4 so less is withheld
questions.intro: Form W-4 controls how much income tax is withheld from each paycheck; you can update it at any time.
questions.feedback: A new W-4 reduces withholding going forward.

misconceptions.B: Can lose refunds and cause problems

questions.prompt: A worker with a side gig owes $900 extra each year. Which approach pays it gradually?

sections.skill: If you cannot pay in full

questions.prompt: Leo owes $560 but can pay only $200 by the deadline. What is the best step?

choices.text: Do not file at all until he can pay every single dollar
File on time, pay $200, and set up a payment plan

questions.correct_answer: File on time, pay $200, and set up a payment plan
questions.intro: The penalty for not filing is usually larger than the penalty for not paying. The IRS offers payment plans (installment agreements). Interest and penalties still apply to unpaid amounts.
questions.feedback: Filing on time avoids the bigger penalty; a payment plan handles the rest.
sources: IRS: Individual returns are generally due April 15 (next business day if on a weekend or holiday); an extension extends the time to file, not to pay; IRS Free File and VITA offer free filing help to eligible taxpayers. (https://www.irs.gov/filing)

questions.prompt: Which penalty is generally LARGER per month: failure to file or failure to pay?

choices.text: Neither exists if a refund is due

questions.intro: The IRS charges separate penalties for filing late and paying late; the late-filing penalty is generally larger.
questions.feedback: Failure-to-file penalties are generally larger, so file on time even if you cannot pay.

questions.prompt: Does a filing extension give more time to PAY taxes owed?

choices.text: Yes, six more months to pay with no interest
No; it extends the time to file, not to pay

questions.correct_answer: No; it extends the time to file, not to pay
questions.intro: An extension (Form 4868) gives more time to file, but any tax owed is still due by the original deadline.
questions.feedback: Tax owed is still due by the April deadline; interest applies after.

questions.prompt: Leo owes $360 and sets up a 6-month payment plan, ignoring interest and fees. What is each payment?
questions.intro: Equal payments = total owed ÷ number of payments.
questions.feedback: $360 ÷ 6 = $60 (interest and fees add a little more).
